mappings.note: Part (a) is convex-mirror image characteristics (LO-1); part (b) demands a concave-mirror construction for the object beyond C, which is the ray-diagram outcome.
The range 0 < u < f comes from the object-position rule for an erect concave-mirror image, not from the mirror formula; the diagram is the second graded step.
m = -1/5 gives u, then the mirror formula gives f - both of LO-2's formulae substituted. The mirror type falls out of the sign, not from an image-location rule.
Magnification then mirror formula then R = 2f, all numeric. Nothing qualitative is asked, so LO-2 alone.
Two sign cases of m = +/-3 run separately through the mirror formula - the distinguishing skill is handling the magnification sign in a substitution, which is LO-2.
Explains retracing by i = r = 0 because the normal passes through C - a law-of-reflection argument. Nothing is drawn, so C 8.1-LO-2 is not cited.
Object range and image size from the inside-the-focus rule (LO-1) plus a required diagram (C 8.1-LO-2). Near-duplicate of the f = 15 cm version; see defect list.
Identifies plane, concave and convex mirrors from the image each gives at close range - LO-1's three named mirror types, used diagnostically.
Constructing rays to locate an unknown lens and its focus; the lens naming rests on the competency's lens-properties clause. Near-duplicate of the part-4 convex version.
Names the mirror for three uses (shaving, ENT, rear-view) and justifies each from the image it forms - applied image characteristics across concave and convex mirrors, with no diagram demanded.
Bent pencil explained by bending away from the normal at a water-air surface (LO-3), with a ray diagram explicitly demanded. C 8.1-LO-2 stretched past its mirrors-and-lenses wording.
States the laws of refraction and applies them to normal incidence on a slab - both halves are LO-3's 'states the laws of refraction' clause; no diagram is required.
Two uses of concave mirrors, justified by the magnified erect image inside the focus - applied image characteristics, LO-1.
A labelled slab refraction diagram is the first graded step; interpreting n = 2.42 is the refractive-index clause of LO-3.
Three unrelated parts: f = R/2 for a mirror sits nearest LO-1, while why n > 1 and the sign of a -4 D lens are both on the refraction/lens side. A composite item that no single code fits.
Optical density inferred from bending away from the normal - the laws of refraction. The 'floats on' detail is a distractor about mass density, not optical density.
Lateral displacement defined and its dependence on slab thickness and refractive index - a refraction result; no diagram is asked for here, unlike the neighbouring slab items.
Drawing and labelling i, r, e and the lateral shift is the diagram outcome; giving n = sin i / sin r is the stated law of refraction.
Part (a) demands a diagram that proves the emergent ray is parallel; part (b) is a reciprocal refractive-index calculation. Two separate graded steps.
Ranks two media by their angles of refraction at equal incidence and computes the speed in diamond - laws of refraction plus n = c/v, both in LO-3.
Two magnification sign cases fed through the lens formula for a convex lens - the lens counterpart of the mirror two-case item, so LO-3 and not LO-2.
Reads a table of refractive indices to say where light speeds up and computes a relative index - the refractive-index clause used on data.
Two conditions for no bending and the n-to-velocity relation - a statement item on the laws of refraction and the definition of n.
Lens formula solved for f from given u and v, then magnification judged from where the object sits relative to f - LO-3's lens-formula clause.
Lens formula for u with the image on a screen, plus m = v/u. Lens magnification has no outcome of its own, so LO-3 carries it.
